stories.title: Sisters of the Visitation Monastery Sells to Brooklyn and Miami Developers for $42M
stories.excerpt: A 170-year-old monastery in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, has sold for $42.25 million. The Sisters of the Visitation’s 7.5-acre campus at 8902 Ridge Boulevard –– a campus behind 30-foot stone walls, with a monastery, chapel and school –– was bought by a group of Brooklyn- and Miami-based developers and investors with a history of large residential projects, including leaders of Heights Advisors, Integritas Capital and Royal Palm Companies. A petition by the Catholic religious order to sell its real estate was approved by the office of the New York State Attorney General on Monday. Nonprofits are required by New York law to obtain approval when it sells all or most of its assets. The buyer entity, 1137 91 LLC, is made up of beneficial owners with overlapping development and investment firms. Those include Brooklyn real estate investor Stephen Palmese, founder of private equity platform Integritas Capital (and a former vice chair at JLL), and Rachel Foster, founder and president of Brooklyn housing developer Heights Advisors, alongside the developer’s director, Scott Geddes. The longtime professional partners are planning a resort-residential tower in Fort Lauderdale, according to The Real Deal. Palmese’s Integritas is also the lender behind a forthcoming 27-story church-to-residential conversion in Brooklyn’s Fort Greene. Also named in the LLC is Daniel Kodsi, CEO of Miami developer Royal Palm Companies. A fifth owner, Matthew Kodsi, is an undergraduate student who has worked part-time at Heights Advisors. The cohort of buyers suggests the historic property’s likely fate as a major mixed-used or residential development. The Visitation Sisters entered into an initial contract in late April, according to the filing, but the school and monastery have been shuttered since 2024, after their numbers dropped too low to sustain full ministry. bullets: Sisters of Visitation Monastery, Bay Ridge Brooklyn, sold for $42.25M to Heights Advisors/Integritas/Royal Palm.
7.5-acre campus includes monastery, chapel, school behind 30-foot walls; zoned/entitlement status unclear from text.
Buyer group has track record large residential projects; potential conversion to apartments or mixed-use.
stories.summary: A 170-year-old, 7.5-acre religious campus in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn sold for $42.25M to a developer consortium led by Heights Advisors, Integritas Capital, and Royal Palm Companies. The site sits behind 30-foot stone walls and includes a monastery, chapel, and school. The sale required New York State Attorney General approval under nonprofit asset-sale law. The buyer entity (1137 91 LLC) has a history of large residential development.
stories.impact: Bay Ridge has limited large-format land for residential—this 7.5-acre institutional hold becomes a potential anchor for significant new supply. Entitlement and zoning pathway will determine whether the group can deliver 150–300+ units; if achievable, it could shift Bay Ridge's rental trajectory and cap-rate compression in Brooklyn outer boroughs. Monitor conversion feasibility and community opposition.

stories.title: Benefit Street Partners Provides $103M Bridge Debt for Texas Multifamily Portfolio
stories.excerpt: Vantage Communities has secured $103 million in bridge debt to refinance a three-property, 864-unit multifamily portfolio in three cities in Texas, Commercial Observer can first report. Benefit Street Partners provided the debt, which will finance the property toward full stabilization and is structured as a floating-rate, interest-only bridge loan with a three-year term. Greystone Capital Advisors‘ Drew Fletcher, Bryan Grover, Jesse Kopecky and Cameron Behr arranged the transaction. “Benefit Street Partners recognized the quality of the sponsorship, the assets, and the long-term fundamentals supporting these dynamic Central Texas markets,” said Fletcher. The three assets are split among Vantage at Hutto — a 288-unit complex located at 1051 North Farm to Market 1660 in Hutto, Tex., just outside of Austin; Vantage at McKinney Falls — a 288-unit complex located at 7900 McKinney Falls Parkway in suburban Austin, Tex.; and Vantage at Fair Oaks — a 288-unit complex located at 9135 Dietz Elkhorn Road in Boerne, Tex. outside of San Antonio. All three assets opened in either 2023 or 2024 and feature amenities such as resident clubhouses, fitness centers and resort-style swimming pools. “We were pleased to structure a financing solution that met our clients’ objectives while leveraging the strength of this high-quality, recently delivered portfolio,” added Fletcher in a statement. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Vantage Communities secured $103M bridge debt from Benefit Street Partners for 864-unit Texas portfolio.
Three properties: Hutto (288 units), McKinney Falls Austin (288 units), Fair Oaks Boerne (288 units); floating-rate, 3-year term.
Bridge structure signals stabilization play; Central Texas fundamentals strong enough to attract institutional capital.
stories.summary: Vantage Communities closed $103M in bridge debt from Benefit Street Partners to refinance a three-property, 864-unit multifamily portfolio across Central Texas (Hutto, McKinney Falls near Austin, and Boerne). The floating-rate, interest-only loan carries a three-year term and is structured toward full stabilization. Greystone Capital Advisors arranged the deal, citing strong sponsorship and long-term market fundamentals.
stories.impact: Bridge refinancing in Central Texas signals lender confidence in rent trajectory and absorption in Austin's supply-constrained suburbs (Hutto, McKinney Falls). Floating-rate structure bets on rate stability or decline; if rates hold or rise, refinance risk materializes in 2027–2029, tightening capital availability for lesser-sponsored assets. Monitor Austin submarket leasing velocity.

stories.title: Coastland Residential Lands $85M to Build Miami-Dade Rental
stories.excerpt: Coastland Residential has nabbed a $84.5 million construction loan for a multifamily development near Tropical Park in southwest Miami-Dade County. The debt from PNC Bank covers the Vybe 75, which will house 366 apartments and 5,000 square feet of ground-floor retail space. The eight-story development at 4383 Southwest 75th Avenue sits just east of Tropical Park and the Palmetto Expressway, south of Bird Road. At least a portion of the units will be priced within 120 percent of the area’s median income, though a representative for the Pinecrest-based developer declined to provide an exact figure. Amenities will include a rooftop pool, a gym, a co-working lounge, a sports simulator and a movie theater. Coastland Residential purchased the 4.3-acre site for $14.5 million last year, according to property records. The Corwil Architects-designed development represents the first phase of a larger project that’s expected to deliver about 1,000 units in total. Launched five years ago by Anthony Seijas and Alejandro Rodriguez, Coastland Residential grew out of Rodriguez’s contracting and construction management firm, Coastland Construction, which is also serving as the contractor for Vybe 75. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Coastland Residential secured $84.5M construction loan from PNC Bank for 366-unit Vybe 75, southwest Miami-Dade.
Site purchased for $14.5M; first phase of 1,000+ unit master plan; includes 5,000 SF retail, mixed-income (120% AMI floor).
Rooftop amenities (pool, gym, co-working, movie theater) signal class-A positioning in emerging Tropical Park corridor.
stories.summary: Coastland Residential closed $84.5M in construction financing from PNC Bank for Vybe 75, a 366-unit, eight-story multifamily development near Tropical Park in southwest Miami-Dade. The 4.3-acre site, purchased last year for $14.5M, will include 5,000 SF of ground-floor retail and mixed-income units (minimum 120% AMI). Amenities include rooftop pool, gym, co-working space, and movie theater. The project represents phase one of a larger 1,000+ unit pipeline.
stories.impact: Southwest Miami-Dade (Tropical Park/Pinecrest submarket) is seeing institutional capital commit to emerging areas outside saturated coastal zones. Mixed-income mandate and aggressive amenity package suggest developer is competing for workforce and middle-income renters amid Miami's supply glut—signals rent pressure in secondary submarkets. Phase 2 optionality (600+ units) depends on absorption and refinance feasibility of phase 1; construction completion and lease-up timing critical for market fundamentals.

stories.title: Northmarq Arranges Refis for Three Texas Rental Communities
stories.excerpt: Francis Property Management inked a $68.7 million refinancing on three Texas multifamily communities. Northmarq’s Debt + Equity deal team led by Taylor Francis, along with David Blum, Joe Giordani, Charlie Buckingham and Matt Radich arranged the permanent fixed-rate financing for the three-property Class A multifamily portfolio totaling 940 units located in Houston and San Antonio, Texas. Each loan was structured on a 10-year term with full-term interest-only payments. Holden Heights (shown) is a 282-unit mid-rise apartment community in Houston’s highly desirable Heights neighborhood. Built in 2015, the property features one- and two-bedroom floor plans with community amenities that incudeo a pool, wellness center, and a landscaped courtyard. Estancia San Miguel is a 300-unit garden-style community situated in Houston’s Cypress/Fairbanks submarket. Built in 2006, the property features one-, two- and three-bedroom floor plans with amenities that include a swimming pool, clubhouse, business center and on-site laundry facilities. The Montecristo Apartments is a 358-unit garden-style community strategically positioned along North Loop 1604 East within San Antonio’s Far North Central submarket. Built in 2005, the property offers private balconies and fireplaces in select floor plans. Join the region’s leading multifamily owners, developers, investors, lenders, and brokers at Connect Texas Multifamily on August 13 in Dallas for a focused discussion on the market forces redefining Texas real estate. bullets: Francis Property Management refinanced $68.7M on three Texas multifamily properties (940 units) via Northmarq permanent fixed-rate debt.
Holden Heights Houston (282 units, 2015), Estancia San Miguel Cypress (300 units, 2006), Montecristo San Antonio (358 units, 2005).
10-year term, interest-only throughout; refinance from construction/bridge debt indicates strong stabilization and local rent growth.
stories.summary: Northmarq arranged $68.7M in permanent fixed-rate refinancing for Francis Property Management's three-property, 940-unit multifamily portfolio across Houston and San Antonio. The deal includes Holden Heights (282 units, mid-rise, Heights submarket), Estancia San Miguel (300 units, garden-style, Cypress/Fairbanks), and Montecristo (358 units, garden-style, San Antonio's Far North Central). Each loan is structured on a 10-year term with full-term interest-only payments.
stories.impact: Permanent fixed-rate closing on 5–20 year old assets signals lender conviction on Houston/San Antonio rent stability and cap-rate floor. Interest-only terms indicate expectation of sustained rent growth; alternative would be amortizing if market were softening. This refinancing reduces portfolio refinance risk in 2027–2029, freeing sponsor capital for acquisitions or development. Monitor trailing lease spreads in Houston Heights and Cypress to confirm absorption strength.

stories.title: North American Data Center Demand Reaches All-Time High
stories.excerpt: North America data center demand reached an all-time high in the first half of 2026, with 25 gigawatts of absorption, double the level from a year ago and five times that of two years prior. JLL’s North America Data Center Report – Midyear 2026 says that although structural demand continues to accelerate, responsible growth now depends on building trust through transparency and early community engagement around electricity, water and noise impacts. Seventy-nine percent of Americans support U.S. leadership in artificial intelligence, while only 14% support data center development in their communities. The 65-point support gap threatens to constrain the infrastructure buildout required to maintain AI competitiveness, the report states. “We’re witnessing demand levels that continue to exceed even industry insiders’ expectations,” said Andy Cvengros, executive managing director, co-lead of U.S. Data Center Markets, JLL. “The market absorbed 25 gigawatts in just six months, driven by hyperscalers, neoclouds and pure-play AI companies competing aggressively for scarce capacity. But the real story is how community acceptance, or lack thereof, has emerged as the defining challenge for this next phase of growth. The industry and communities need to come together to find a path forward that benefits everyone.” The post North American Data Center Demand Reaches All-Time High appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: North America data center absorption hit 25 GW in H1 2026, double prior year, driven by AI hyperscalers and neoclouds.
79% of Americans support U.S. AI leadership; only 14% support local data center development—65-point gap threatens infrastructure buildout.
Community acceptance emerging as primary constraint; electricity, water, noise impacts require transparency and early engagement.
stories.summary: JLL reports North American data center demand reached an all-time high in H1 2026, with 25 gigawatts of absorption—double the prior year and five times the level two years prior. Demand driven by hyperscalers, neoclouds, and AI companies competing for scarce capacity. However, a stark gap exists: 79% of Americans support U.S. AI leadership, but only 14% support data center development in their communities, creating a 65-point support gap that threatens required infrastructure expansion.
stories.impact: Explosive data center demand growth is indirectly bullish for multifamily in Tier-2 and Tier-3 metros with data center clusters (e.g., Virginia, Phoenix, Ohio, Texas)—those markets will see tech worker in-migration and job growth, lifting apartment demand and rent velocity. However, community opposition to data centers may slow buildout, constraining job growth in some regions. Developers should flag metros with friendly zoning/permitting for data center projects as emerging demand drivers, and anticipate multifamily supply shortages if data center approvals slow.

stories.title: Cedarwood Building 272-Unit Celina Rental Community
stories.excerpt: Cedarwood Companies is advancing Topaz at Light Farms Way, a 272-unit multifamily community in Celina. The development will feature a mix of studio, one-bedroom and two-bedroom apartments. Residents will enjoy a clubhouse with a cybercafé, a pool with a fire pit, a fitness center, a dedicated dog park with a pet spa, a playground, a car care center, plus walking trails. Construction on the apartments is set to begin soon, and residents are expected to start moving in next summer,  Founded in 1972, Cedarwood still continues to have many multifamily community projects and has expanded on some of its existing projects to include additional neighborhoods. Their project base has also expanded to include senior living communities and self-storage facilities. Move-ins are expected to begin in summer 2027. Cedarwood, founded in 1972, has expanded its portfolio to include senior living and self-storage.
stories.impact: Celina (Collin County, north Dallas exurb) is a high-growth satellite market attracting families and remote workers seeking affordable space and new construction. This 272-unit delivery adds to DFW's supply pipeline in a submarket experiencing rapid appreciation; monitor absorption pace to confirm demand keeps pace with new completions. If Celina stabilizes strongly, it signals expansion opportunity for competitors in similar DFW and North Texas exurb corridors.

stories.title: Too Big to Burn: L.A. Takes Harder Look at Megawarehouses After Cold Storage Fire
stories.excerpt: A person rides a bicycle as a massive warehouse fire at a Lineage cold storage facility burns on June 20 in Los Angeles. PHOTO: Mario Tama/Getty Images The smells still coming from the husk of the Lineage Cold Storage warehouse, which caught fire in the Boyle Heights neighborhood of Los Angeles on June 17, defy common description. Nearly 4,000 odor complaints have been lodged with the South Coast Air Quality Management District (SCAQMD), with various descriptions of the putrid smell of rotting meat and other food. During a SCAQMD hearing in August, L.A. Mayor Karen Bass said “the putrid offensive odor coming from the tens of millions of pounds of rotting food in the warehouse is unbearable. … Now flies, rats and other pests have infested the community.” In addition to picking up the funky scent, local leaders are also starting to express significant concern and unease around these projects, and their location adjacent to residential neighborhoods. When Lineage submitted plans to rebuild the half-million-square-foot building in late July, it led to outcry from L.A. leaders. In that same SCAQMD statement, Mayor Bass, who issued an emergency executive order placing a hold on rebuilding until cleanup is complete, urged the SCAQMD to hold Lineage “accountable to the maximum extent of the law. That includes fines, effective mitigation, and a complete and thorough cleanup,” including “maximum penalties for the ongoing air quality violations, including maximum financial fines.” Councilmember Ysabel Jurado has advocated for a suite of environmental justice ordinances in wake of the fire, including an ordinance that would prohibit locating new cold storage warehouses anywhere near school, daycares and other sensitive sites. bullets: Lineage Cold Storage warehouse fire, Boyle Heights Los Angeles, June 17; nearly 4,000 odor complaints to SCAQMD.
L.A. Mayor Bass cited 'tens of millions of pounds of rotting food,' pest infestation in adjacent residential neighborhoods.
City now scrutinizing megawarehouse siting; rebuilt facility and zoning for future projects may face new restrictions or setbacks.
stories.summary: A Lineage Cold Storage megawarehouse in Boyle Heights, Los Angeles, caught fire on June 17, releasing odor complaints (nearly 4,000 lodged with SCAQMD) and drawing attention to the facility's proximity to residential neighborhoods. L.A. Mayor Karen Bass cited the 'unbearable' odor from tens of millions of pounds of rotting food and resulting pest infestation. Local leaders are now expressing significant concern about megawarehouses adjacent to residential areas, and Lineage's plans to rebuild are facing heightened scrutiny.
stories.impact: This event is NOT directly relevant to multifamily development but signals tightening land-use regulation in L.A. that could indirectly constrain industrial and logistics growth near residential zones, potentially limiting job growth in those submarkets. However, if city tightens warehouse siting, it may preserve or upgrade nearby residential submarkets (e.g., Boyle Heights, East L.A.) by reducing industrial nuisance, potentially creating uplift demand for apartment redevelopment or new infill multifamily. Monitor L.A. zoning amendments and their impact on industrial land supply and neighborhood residential desirability.

stories.title: Northwestern Mutual Provides $110M Perm Loan for Jersey City Multifamily Tower
stories.excerpt: A joint venture between Spitzer Enterprises and Arden Group has sealed $109.5 million of permanent financing for a newly-built multifamily tower in Jersey City, Commercial Observer can first report. Northwestern Mutual supplied the loan to retire construction debt following the lease-up and stabilization of 2024-completed, 390-unit 425 Summit development in Jersey City’s Journal Square neighborhood. CBRE arranged the transaction with a debt & structured finance team consisting of Matthew Pizzolato, Jason Gaccione, Jake Salkovitz, Shawn Rosenthal, Josh Stein and Carlos Silva. “425 Summit represented a compelling opportunity to finance a recently stabilized, institutional-quality multifamily asset in one of the region’s most dynamic residential markets,” Pizzolato said in a statement. “Because of the property’s exceptional transit connectivity, quality construction, strong operating performance and experienced sponsorship, there was no shortage of interest from the lending community.” Located at 425 Summit Avenue less than a half mile from the Journal Square Path station, the 27-story building has studio to three-bedroom apartments and is 98 percent leased, according to CBRE. The property has ground-floor retail space along with community amenities that include a fitness center, coworking lounge, golf simulator and pet spa. Northwestern Mutual, Spitzer Enterprises and Arden Group did not immediately return requests for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Northwestern Mutual provided $109.5M permanent financing for Spitzer Enterprises/Arden Group's 425 Summit, Jersey City, 390 units.
2024-completed, 390-unit development in Journal Square, Jersey City; transit-connected, recently stabilized and lease-up.
CBRE arranged; lenders cited institutional-quality asset, experienced sponsorship, strong operating performance; fixed-rate perm loan retires construction debt.
stories.summary: A joint venture between Spitzer Enterprises and Arden Group closed $109.5M in permanent financing from Northwestern Mutual for 425 Summit, a newly-completed, 390-unit multifamily tower in Jersey City's Journal Square neighborhood. The loan retires construction debt following lease-up and stabilization in 2024. CBRE arranged the transaction, citing the property's exceptional transit connectivity, quality construction, strong operating performance, and experienced sponsorship.
stories.impact: Jersey City Journal Square has become a financing magnet for institutional lenders—permanent debt on 390-unit, class-A, transit-accessible multifamily closes readily at scale, signaling strong rent fundamentals and low-risk operational profile. This signals cap-rate compression in Jersey City Core and continued flight-to-quality in the region. Developers should prioritize transit-connected Jersey City sites; non-transit assets or secondary markets may face refinance or acquisition headwinds.

stories.title: VanTrust Starts Work on 512K-SF McKinney Warehouse Venture
stories.excerpt: VanTrust Real Estate has begun construction on Phase 1 of 121 Commerce Park, the company’s first industrial park in McKinney. Phase 1 will include more than 512,000 square feet of Class A industrial space across two speculative buildings. Phase 1 includes Building A, totaling 242,393 square feet, and Building B, totaling 270,479 square feet. Both buildings are designed with flexible single- or multi-tenant configurations. Completion is anticipated in the second quarter of 2027. Situated on 42 acres at the northwest corner of Tina Drive and SH-121, 121 Commerce Park offers direct access to U.S. 75, State Highway 121/Sam Rayburn Tollway and Highway 380, with convenient proximity to McKinney National Airport. Future plans also call for an additional 250,000 square feet of build-to-suit industrial space in Phase 2 . JLL’s Kurt Griffin and Nathan Orbin market the project. VanTrust has selected Evans General Contractors, GSR Andrade Architects and Kimley-Horn to support the development of 121 Commerce Park. bullets: VanTrust Real Estate began Phase 1 of 121 Commerce Park, McKinney, Texas: 512,000 SF industrial space across two buildings.

stories.summary: VanTrust Real Estate began construction on Phase 1 of 121 Commerce Park, its first industrial park in McKinney, Texas. Phase 1 includes 512,000 SF of Class A industrial space across two speculative buildings (242K SF Building A, 270K SF Building B) with flexible single- or multi-tenant configurations. Completion is anticipated in Q2 2027. The 42-acre site offers direct access to U.S. 75, SH-121, and Highway 380, with proximity to McKinney National Airport. Phase 2 will add up to 250,000 SF of build-to-suit industrial space.
stories.impact: NOT directly multifamily-relevant, but McKinney is a logistics and light-industrial hub feeding DFW growth. Industrial buildout signals job creation and employer activity; if tenants occupy Phase 1 and expand into Phase 2, McKinney will see wage-earning worker in-migration supporting apartment demand. Monitor lease-up pace and tenant profiles (3PLs, last-mile, manufacturing) to forecast multifamily demand in McKinney's rental market.

stories.title: Value, Nostalgia and Gas Prices Shape Store Traffic in 2026
stories.excerpt: With gas prices climbing sharply, inflation on the rise again, and economic uncertainty weighing on discretionary budgets, the first half of 2026 put consumers to the test, Placer.ai reports in a new white paper. However, the impact of more pain at the pump was not as generalized as one might think. In the new white paper, The Forces Shaping Consumer Traffic in 2026, Placer.ai notes that higher gas prices reshuffled consumer activity rather than merely slowing it down. Dining establishments were hit harder than brick-and-mortar retailers, although long-distance destination retail felt some of the impact. The white paper also examines how the value proposition is driving both store traffic and growth in store traffic. At the same time, nostalgia for early 2000s mall mainstays is also powering growth for the brands in a position to capitalize on it. “Barnes & Noble may have been the original heritage brand comeback story, and its continued strength in H1 2026 suggests the nostalgia wave has yet to reach its peak,” Placer.ai reports. The post Value, Nostalgia and Gas Prices Shape Store Traffic in 2026 appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: H1 2026: gas prices climbing, inflation rising, economic uncertainty weighing on consumer discretionary budgets per Placer.ai.
Higher gas prices reshuffled consumer activity; dining establishments hit harder than brick-and-mortar retail; long-distance destination retail also impacted.
Value proposition and nostalgia (early 2000s mall brands, e.g., Barnes & Noble resurgence) driving traffic growth among some retailers.
stories.summary: Placer.ai reports that H1 2026 consumer traffic was shaped by gas price increases, rising inflation, and economic uncertainty. Higher fuel costs did not uniformly slow foot traffic; instead, they reshuffled consumer activity—dining establishments were hit harder than brick-and-mortar retailers, while long-distance destination retail felt some impact. The report notes that value proposition and nostalgia for early 2000s mall anchors (e.g., Barnes & Noble) are powering traffic growth for brands positioned to capitalize.
stories.impact: NOT directly multifamily-relevant, but signals consumer income stress (rising inflation, gas costs, uncertainty) could soften rental demand in discretionary-focused markets if household formation or mobility slows. However, value-seeking behavior is positive for workforce and middle-income multifamily. Monitor regional employment and wage growth; if consumer traffic patterns reveal geographic spending weakness, multifamily demand may soften in those metros. Conversely, value-oriented retail growth may correlate with stable workforce housing demand in cost-conscious submarkets.
